title: Johns Hopkins: Alzheimer's Brain Shrinkage Precedes Memory Loss by Years
summary: Johns Hopkins researchers found that the entorhinal cortex and amygdala begin shrinking up to a decade before Alzheimer's disease causes memory loss, linked to abnormal tau protein buildup. This discovery could enable earlier detection and treatment before extensive brain damage occurs.
takeaways: Brain shrinkage detected 5–10 years before Alzheimer's memory symptoms appear
Entorhinal cortex and amygdala affected earlier than hippocampus
Changes linked to abnormal tau protein buildup
Earlier detection could allow treatment when it has greatest potential to protect brain

title: AI Discovers Hidden Heart Signal Predicting Sudden Cardiac Death

The algorithm identified patients with 7% annual death risk versus 4.6% using standard methods, and flagged broader high-ri
takeaways: AI system trained on 440,000 EKGs from Sweden, validated in US and Taiwan
AI-identified group shows 7% annual sudden cardiac death rate vs 4.6% conventionally
Algorithm detects broader high-risk populations missed by existing guidelines
Works with ordinary EKG images already routinely collected in hospitals

title: Stanford researchers discover brain activity patterns predicting Alzheimer's years early
summary: Stanford researchers discovered that subtle brain activity patterns can predict Alzheimer's disease risk years before memory problems or protein buildup occurs. takeaways: Study published Nov 4, 2026, in Science Advances
Brain activity patterns predicted cognitive decline more effectively than demographics, genetics, amyloid-beta, tau biomarkers
Cohort: adults 55–70 assessed; follow-up periods extended to 12 years
Participants with Alzheimer's-like patterns more likely to experience decline, accumulate amyloid-beta, receive Alzheimer's diagnosis
Super ager patterns associated with maintained cognitive abilities and avoided outcomes
Unlike conventional biomarkers, brain patterns may be modifiable via cognitive training and transcranial magnetic stimulation

title: Yale study reveals prescription drugs and exercise slow aging; supplements ineffective
summary: Yale researchers analyzing 51 studies found that certain prescription drugs, healthy diets, and exercise can measurably slow biological aging markers, while popular over-the-counter supplements showed little effect. takeaways: Analyzed 51 studies on anti-aging interventions
Measured using DNA-based blood tests for biological aging
Prescription drugs, healthy diet, and exercise showed measurable effects
Popular over-the-counter anti-aging supplements largely ineffective
Changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean longer lifespan or disease avoidance

title: Large pregnancy study shows Ozempic and Wegovy linked to premature birth risk when used for diabetes
summary: A Danish study of 756,636 pregnancies found that GLP-1 drugs (semaglutide, liraglutide) were not linked to increased pregnancy complications when prescribed for weight loss. However, when prescribed for diabetes, early exposure was associated with higher premature birth risk, likely driven by diabet
takeaways: Study of 756,636 pregnancies in Denmark (Oct 2009–Dec 2023)
No increased complications when GLP-1s used for weight loss
Higher premature birth risk (before 37 weeks) with diabetes prescriptions
Published in Human Reproduction Open
Current clinical guidance: stop GLP-1s 8 weeks before pregnancy planning
Guidance based on early-phase lab studies, not real-world evidence
Diabetes, not medication, likely drives premature birth risk

title: Energy drinks linked to 11× higher cardiac arrest reports in new study
summary: A study presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 found energy drinks and stimulant supplements associated with 11× more cardiac arrest reports and 4.5× more heart attack reports. Young adults ages 18–34 comprised nearly half of severe cases; some products contain 3–12×
takeaways: Energy drinks/stimulants vs. products without: 11× cardiac arrest reports, 4.5× heart attack reports

title: United States at risk of losing measles elimination status due to ongoing outbreaks
summary: The United States faces potential loss of its measles elimination status following recent outbreaks. A WHO regional committee is expected to decide this week whether the U.S. retains the status it achieved in 2000.
takeaways: At least 8 measles deaths reported in 2026
Decision expected from Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) committee this week
Loss of status previously described as unavoidable consequence of transmission patterns

title: Supervised Rehabilitation Exercise Program May Prevent Early Osteoarthritis After ACL Surgery
summary: A La Trobe University trial with 184 adults aged 18–40 found that a four-month supervised rehabilitation program improved pain, muscle strength, and quality of life after ACL surgery without evidence of cartilage damage. Results published in Annals of Internal Medicine challenge concerns that exerci
takeaways: Trial: 184 adults aged 18–40; 1–3 years post-ACL reconstruction with persistent symptoms
Intervention: four-month progressive exercise therapy and education
Outcomes: improved pain, muscle strength, quality of life; no cartilage damage or worsening early osteoarthritis
Background: ~50% of ACL patients develop early-onset knee osteoarthritis within decade (often before age 40)
Study significance: first to evaluate combined exercise therapy 9+ months post-surgery

title: Study reveals viral infections cause lasting immune system damage despite symptom resolution
summary: Research at Pompeu Fabra University found that mice recovering from acute viral infections experienced lasting immune system damage despite eliminating the virus. takeaways: Study published in Cell Death & Disease
Lasting immune damage observed despite viral clearance
Spleen changes included fibrosis and disrupted immune cell positioning
T cell activation impaired
Pre-infection vaccination prevented harmful immune system changes

title: Stopping statins after age 70 may be safer than expected, but long-term risks remain
summary: A study of nearly 1,900 adults aged 70+ found stopping statins appeared relatively safe short-term for people without prior heart attacks or strokes, but longer-term follow-up revealed higher rates of serious cardiovascular events or death. takeaways: Study of ~1,900 adults aged 70+
Primary prevention without prior cardiovascular events
All participants had ≥2 chronic conditions
Follow-up: ~2 years, some extending to 4 years
Short-term discontinuation appears relatively safe
Longer follow-up: higher serious CV events/death rate
American Heart Association 2026 guideline recommends lifestyle, potentially medication for younger people

title: Occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher stroke risk
